Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The Institute for Supply Management (ISM) announced on July 1, 2024, that its manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) registered 48.5% for June 2024, marking the third consecutive month of contraction in the U.S. manufacturing sector. The report, issued by Timothy R. Fiore, chair of the ISM manufacturing business survey committee, also showed declines in key sub-indexes. The Production Index fell into contraction at 48.5%, a 1.7 percentage point decrease from May, and the Employment Index also dropped to 49.3%, down 1.8 points. In a slight positive movement, the New Orders Index rose by 3.9 percentage points to 49.3%, though it remained in contraction territory. <2> In May 2024, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index remained unchanged, marking the smallest monthly change in six months, with the annual rate slowing to 2.6%. The core PCE price index, which excludes food and energy and is the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation, saw a modest increase of 0.1% for the month. The year-over-year core PCE inflation rate fell to 2.6%, its lowest level since March 2021. <3> The University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index officially fell to a final reading of 65.6 in June 2024, marking its lowest level in seven months. The final results were published on June 28, 2024. The decline from May's index of 69.1 was primarily driven by consumer concerns regarding the impact of high prices, elevated interest rates, and weakening income growth on their personal finances. [2] Many consumers expressed worries about the confluence of high borrowing costs and prices, which created an unfavorable environment, particularly for homebuyers. <4> The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) concluded its two-day meeting on June 12, 2024, announcing it would maintain the federal funds rate at the current range of 5.25% to 5.50%. This decision marked the seventh consecutive meeting where the committee opted to hold rates steady, keeping them at a 23-year high. Concurrently, the FOMC released its updated Summary of Economic Projections, which signaled a significant shift in outlook. Policymakers now anticipate only one quarter-point rate cut for the remainder of 2024, a notable reduction from the three cuts projected in March. The committee's statement noted "modest further progress" toward its 2% inflation goal but indicated that it still requires "greater confidence" that inflation is decreasing sustainably before reducing rates. <5> The U.S. economy added 272,000 jobs in May, significantly surpassing economists' forecasts of 180,000. This strong job growth was accompanied by a slight increase in the unemployment rate, which rose to 4.0% from 3.9% in the previous month. Additionally, average hourly earnings increased by 0.4%, exceeding the anticipated 0.3% rise. [1, 8, 19] <6> The U.S. international trade deficit for goods and services expanded to $74.6 billion in April 2024, an increase of $6.0 billion from a revised $68.6 billion in March. [1] This growth in the deficit was a result of imports rising more significantly than exports. [2] Specifically, April imports were $338.2 billion, which is $8.0 billion more than the previous month, while exports saw a smaller increase of $2.1 billion to reach $263.7 billion. [1] A primary driver of the surge in imports was automotive vehicles, parts, and engines, which saw an increase of $3.9 billion. [2] <7> In its "second" estimate for the first quarter of 2024, the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) reported that U.S. real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) increased at an annual rate of 1.3%. This represents a notable slowdown from the 3.4% growth observed in the fourth quarter of 2023. The announcement was made on May 30, 2024. <8> On May 1, 2024, the U.S. Department of the Treasury announced its quarterly refunding plan, increasing the total auction package to $125 billion for the May to July quarter to refund approximately $107.8 billion in maturing securities and raise $17.2 billion in new cash. The refunding package includes $58 billion in 3-year notes, $42 billion in 10-year notes, and $25 billion in 30-year bonds. Concurrently, the Treasury launched a new securities buyback program to improve liquidity in the bond market. The first buyback operation was scheduled for May 29, 2024. The program involves weekly buybacks of up to $2 billion in nominal coupon securities and up to $500 million in Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS). <9> Compensation costs for U.S. civilian workers increased by 1.2% for the three-month period ending in March 2024, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' Employment Cost Index (ECI) report. [2, 3, 4] This was an acceleration from the 0.9% increase in the previous quarter. [5] For the quarter, wages and salaries rose by 1.1% and benefit costs also increased by 1.1%. [2, 4, 5] Over the 12-month period ending in March 2024, compensation costs for civilian workers increased by 4.2%, which was down from a 4.8% increase for the 12 months ending in March 2023. [2, 3, 4] The data indicated persistent wage pressures, with the quarterly gain being the strongest in a year. [5] <10> During a panel discussion at the Wilson Center, Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell indicated that persistently high inflation would likely delay any potential interest rate cuts. He stated that recent data had not increased confidence in inflation moving towards the central bank's 2% target, suggesting it will likely take "longer than expected" to achieve that goal. Powell further emphasized that if higher inflation continues, the Federal Reserve is prepared to maintain the current high-interest rates for "as long as needed."

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On November 17, 2025, a technical market analysis forecasted a bearish trend for the USD/CHF exchange rate, predicting potential declines toward the 0.7382 to 0.7599 range. This outlook was heavily influenced by central bank actions and U.S.-Swiss trade developments; specifically, a recent trade agreement between the United States and Switzerland helped ease the strength of the Swiss franc, potentially reducing the need for intervention by the Swiss National Bank. <2> The USD/CHF exchange rate dropped below the 0.8000 level as the Swiss Franc gained strength following reports that Switzerland was nearing an agreement with the United States. Under the newly announced framework, the U.S. will lower tariffs on Swiss exports to a ceiling of 15%, a significant reduction from the punitive 39% rate that was imposed by the Trump administration in August 2025. <3> On November 5, 2025, the USD to CHF exchange rate reached a peak of approximately 0.8104, marking the highest rate for the U.S. Dollar against the Swiss Franc over a six-month period. <4> The Federal Reserve enacted its second consecutive interest rate cut on October 29, 2025, lowering the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to a target range of 3.75% to 4.00%. This move, aimed at stimulating the economy by making borrowing cheaper, signals a more accommodative monetary policy. The decision came amidst a mixed economic landscape, with concerns over a softening labor market and elevated inflation, which stood at 3% for the 12 months ending in September 2025. Compounding this complex picture, the National Association of Realtors reported that US pending home sales for September 2025 showed no change from the previous month. This stagnation in the housing market, despite falling mortgage rates, pointed to continued weakness in the sector. While the Federal Reserve's rate cut was widely anticipated, Fed Chair Jerome Powell cautioned that a further cut in December was not guaranteed, emphasizing a data-dependent approach for future decisions. <5> The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) announced on October 29, 2025, that it would conclude its quantitative tightening program, the reduction of its aggregate securities holdings, on December 1, 2025. This decision was made alongside a 25 basis point cut to the federal funds rate, setting a new target range of 3.75% to 4%. After December 1, the Fed plans to reinvest all principal payments from its maturing Treasury and agency Mortgage-Backed Securities (MBS), with proceeds from maturing MBS being reinvested into short-term Treasury bills. This move signals a shift from a contractionary monetary policy to a more stable, ample-reserve environment. <6> On October 20, 2025, the U.S. Dollar (USD) declined against the Swiss Franc (CHF), with the USD/CHF exchange rate trading around 0.7925. This weakening of the dollar was primarily influenced by an ongoing U.S. government shutdown that commenced on October 1, 2025, after Congress failed to pass necessary appropriations legislation. The prolonged political stalemate fueled concerns about U.S. economic growth and solidified market expectations for further monetary easing by the Federal Reserve. These expectations were realized later in the month when the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) implemented a 0.25 percentage point interest rate cut, lowering the target range to 3.75%–4.00%. The shutdown, which became the longest in U.S. history, complicated the Fed's decision-making process by delaying the release of key economic data. <7> The University of Michigan's preliminary Consumer Sentiment Index for October was 55.0, virtually unchanged from September's 55.1, according to a report released on October 10, 2025. This figure was slightly above the forecasted 54.2. The report also indicated that consumers' year-ahead inflation expectations edged down to 4.6% from 4.7% in the prior month. The sentiment index reading was described as remaining at a historically low level, representing the third consecutive monthly decline. <8> In a report released on October 3, 2025, the Institute for Supply Management (ISM) announced that its Services Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) registered 50.0% for September 2025. This figure, a decrease from August's 52%, fell short of the forecasted 51.7% and indicated that economic activity in the services sector had stalled. The 50.0% reading represents the exact breakeven point, where a reading above 50 signifies expansion and a reading below 50 indicates contraction. Key components of the report showed that the Business Activity Index fell to 49.9%, entering contraction for the first time since May 2020. While the New Orders Index remained in expansion territory at 50.4%, it slowed from the previous month. The Employment Index continued its contraction for the fourth consecutive month, and price pressures intensified. <9> On September 29, 2025, the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) released statistics on the U.S. international investment position for the second quarter of 2025. The data, reflecting the position at the end of June 2025, showed a net international investment position of -$26.14 trillion. This was a $1.49 trillion change from a revised net position of -$24.65 trillion at the end of the first quarter. Total U.S. assets abroad were valued at $39.56 trillion, while liabilities to foreign residents were $65.71 trillion. The increase in the negative net position was attributed to net financial transactions of -$428.1 billion and other changes, including price and exchange-rate fluctuations, of -$1.06 trillion. <10> Amid growing concerns of a potential U.S. government shutdown, lawmakers faced a critical deadline of September 30 to pass a funding bill. A failure to do so was anticipated to risk the delay of key U.S. economic data releases, including the nonfarm payrolls report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. This looming possibility created significant uncertainty in financial markets and was identified as a contributing factor to the U.S. Dollar's decline against other major currencies.

Prediction target period: from 2026-03-05 to 2026-03-20. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On February 19, 2026, Standard Chartered issued a forecast predicting the USD/CHF exchange rate will fall to 0.75 over the next three months and 0.74 over the next twelve months. The prediction is based on an expected narrowing of the interest rate gap between the US and Switzerland, driven by projected Federal Reserve rate cuts and largely unchanged Swiss policy rates that will erode the US dollar's interest rate advantage. <2> MarketPulse issued a technical analysis report indicating that the USD/CHF pair was carving out a bottom near the 0.7650 level after reaching 14-year lows. The report noted that the pair was breaking out from a mid-February triangle consolidation, driven by heavy Swiss deflationary pressures contrasting with extreme US dollar bearish positioning in the broader market. <3> In January 2026, the Swiss Consumer Price Index (CPI) contracted by 0.1% compared to the previous month. Following the release of these negative figures, the USD/CHF currency pair climbed back above the 0.7700 level. Despite this rebound, the pair remained on track for an overall weekly decline as market traders awaited upcoming US CPI data. <4> The USD/CHF pair experienced an intraday bounce after the delayed release of the US January Nonfarm Payrolls (NFP) data on February 11, 2026. Initially scheduled for February 6, the report was postponed due to a partial government shutdown. The data revealed a surprisingly strong addition of 130,000 jobs, significantly beating consensus estimates of approximately 70,000. This resilient labor market data pushed back expectations for near-term Federal Reserve rate cuts from the spring to July, prompting the immediate market reaction. <5> Daily Forex reported that the USD/CHF exchange rate experienced elevated volatility, consolidating and wavering near the 0.7800 level. This market action was driven by active 'jawboning' from the Swiss National Bank (SNB), which explicitly stated its readiness to intervene in foreign exchange markets to talk down the excessively strengthened Swiss franc and prevent the currency from getting out of control. <6> The USD/CHF exchange rate remained steady around 0.7750 despite the release of a disappointing US ADP Employment Change report, which indicated that private sector jobs increased by only 22,000 compared to the anticipated 48,000. <7> A market analysis reported that the USD/CHF pair plummeted toward 14-to-15-year lows at the start of 2026, driven by heightened U.S. Dollar volatility and shifting market dynamics. The Swiss Franc experienced significant inflows as investors actively utilized the currency for carry trade diversification, favoring it over the Japanese Yen due to structural differences. Furthermore, the Franc's appeal was bolstered as investors consistently sought a highly credible safe-haven asset amidst broader economic uncertainty and geopolitical instability. <8> On January 28, 2026, the USD to CHF exchange rate fell to a notable low, with one U.S. Dollar worth approximately 0.7631 Swiss francs (often cited as 0.7632). This significant decline reflected a persistent bearish structure and ongoing selling pressure against the U.S. Dollar. <9> The USD/CHF exchange rate broke its ascending trend as the Swiss Franc benefited from safe-haven flows amid renewed geopolitical tensions. These market movements followed U.S. President Donald Trump's threat to impose tariffs on several European countries, including Denmark and the UK. Trump stated that the tariffs would remain until an agreement was reached for the complete purchase of Greenland by the United States. This aggressive diplomatic move raised widespread concerns over NATO alliance unity, as experts warned that U.S. coercion against an allied nation like Denmark could jeopardize the foundational mutual defense of the transatlantic alliance. <10> The USD/CHF currency pair fell decisively below the 0.8000 psychological level, approaching 14-year lows. This significant downward movement was driven by safe-haven demand for the Swiss Franc amid rising global geopolitical tensions. The shift was further accelerated by notable U.S. Dollar weakness and capital outflows following the Justice Department's announcement that federal prosecutors had opened a criminal investigation into Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell.
